draft.title: Lighting and colour in film
card: Filmmakers choose how a scene is lit. Lighting is one of the first things that tells a viewer how to feel about a place or a character.
Light that is strong and spread evenly, with few dark patches. It tends to feel safe, open and honest, because nothing is hidden.
Little light, with deep dark areas beside bright ones. It tends to create mystery or threat, because the viewer cannot see everything.
Colour works with light. Warm colours such as soft gold can feel cosy. Cold colours such as pale blue can feel distant or uneasy. Viewers may read these differently, so look at the whole scene.
draft.remember: Bright, even light tends to feel safe and open. Dim light with shadows tends to feel mysterious or threatening.

a.q: A film shows a child walking down a hallway. Most of it is dark, and one lamp throws long shadows on the walls. What effect does this lighting most likely have?
opts: It creates mystery or a sense of threat
It makes the hallway feel safe and open
It shows that nothing is hidden from the viewer
It makes the scene feel cheerful and welcoming
a.why: Dim light with strong shadows hides parts of the space, so the viewer wonders what is there. That builds mystery or threat. Bright, even light is the kind that feels safe and open.
a.clue: Think about what the dark areas hide from the viewer.

b.q: In one film, Mia arrives at her new school in clear, even morning light, and the corridors are bright and soft gold. Later, her classmate Leo waits in a room lit by a single lamp, with half his face in shadow. Which reading of the lighting is most reasonable?
opts: Mia's scenes feel safe, Leo seems mysterious or a threat
Mia's scenes feel threatening, Leo seems open and honest
Both scenes feel safe, as all films light scenes the same
Both scenes feel mysterious, as colour matters more than light
b.why: Clear, even, warm light tends to feel safe and open, so Mia's arrival feels welcoming. Leo's single lamp and half-hidden face create shadows, which suggest mystery or threat. The reversed reading mixes up the two effects.
b.clue: Match each lighting style to the feeling it tends to create.
